subject: Computer Networking
title: SFP Transceivers
description: A quick, practical guide to SFP Transceivers.

hook.text: Switches have empty slots that accept hot-pluggable modules. Those modules are SFP transceivers.

buildup.text: SFP — Small Form-factor Pluggable — converts electrical signals to optical or vice versa.

discovery.text: Different SFPs support different speeds: SFP is 1G, SFP+ is 10G, SFP28 is 25G, QSFP28 is 100G.

twist.text: Swap SFPs without powering down. Change copper to fiber or short-range to long-range in seconds.

climax.text: One switch model works everywhere — data centers, campuses, or long-haul links. Just swap the SFP.

punchline.text: SFP modules make network hardware endlessly adaptable.

quiz.question: What does an SFP transceiver do?
options: Converts electrical signals to optical or vice versa in a hot-swappable module
Encrypts data before it leaves the switch

details.summary: SFP transceivers are hot-swappable modules that plug into switches and routers to provide different types of network connections. By swapping an SFP module, the same switch port can connect to copper, multi-mode fiber, or single-mode fiber at various speeds and distances.
details.whyItMatters: SFP modules provide port flexibility, letting network engineers adapt connections to different cable types and distances without replacing entire switches. They are essential for modern data center connectivity.
takeaways: SFP modules are hot-swappable optical or copper transceivers
Different modules support different fiber types and distances
QSFP modules handle 40 Gbps and 100 Gbps connections

faq.question: What is the difference between SFP, SFP+, and QSFP?
faq.answer: SFP supports 1 Gbps connections. SFP+ supports 10 Gbps using the same form factor. SFP28 handles 25 Gbps. QSFP+ and QSFP28 are larger modules supporting 40 Gbps and 100 Gbps respectively by using four lanes. Higher-speed modules require compatible switch ports.

faq.question: Can I use third-party SFP modules?
faq.answer: Most switches accept coded third-party SFPs that are significantly cheaper than vendor-branded modules. Some vendors lock ports to their own branded modules, but many support an unsupported-transceiver command to override this. Third-party modules with proper coding work reliably.
